reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
clinicalPearls: Biliary hamartomas (von Meyenburg complexes) are benign, usually incidental lesions representing a ductal plate malformation of the small interlobular bile ducts.
They are typically multiple, small, and scattered throughout both lobes, and are almost always asymptomatic with normal liver biochemistry.
On MRI they appear as numerous tiny cystic foci of uniform small size that do not communicate with the biliary tree, best shown on heavily T2-weighted and MRCP sequences.
Their multiplicity and small size can closely mimic hepatic metastases or microabscesses, a critical consideration in patients with known malignancy.
Ultrasound may show tiny hyperechoic or hypoechoic foci sometimes with comet-tail artefact from the dilated ductules.
They lie within the fibropolycystic liver disease spectrum and may coexist with polycystic liver or kidney disease and Caroli disease.
MRCP is the key investigation to confirm the diagnosis non-invasively and avoid unnecessary intervention.
Malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma is exceedingly rare but has been reported, so significant interval change warrants review.
reference.pathophysiology: Von Meyenburg complexes arise from an arrest in the remodelling of the ductal plate, the embryonic template from which the intrahepatic bile ducts form. The result is small clusters of disorganised, variably dilated and often tortuous bile ductules embedded in an abundant fibrous or fibrocollagenous stroma, situated in or adjacent to the portal tracts. The ductules may contain inspissated bile but characteristically do not communicate with the functioning biliary tree, which accounts for their cystic appearance on imaging without biliary dilatation. Because the underlying defect is one of ductal plate malformation, biliary hamartomas share pathogenesis with the wider fibropolycystic spectrum, including congenital hepatic fibrosis, Caroli disease, and autosomal dominant polycystic disease, with which they frequently coexist.
additionalInvestigations: MRI with MRCP as the key confirmatory study
abdominal ultrasound including assessment for comet-tail artefact
contrast-enhanced CT to assess enhancement pattern
renal imaging to assess for associated polycystic kidney disease
liver biopsy reserved for genuinely indeterminate lesions
redFlags: an enlarging lesion or one developing a mural nodule or solid component
obstructive jaundice, which points to an alternative diagnosis
new dominant mass distinct from the uniform hamartomatous pattern
rising tumour markers in the appropriate clinical context
reference.prognosis: The lesions are benign with an excellent prognosis and generally require no treatment. Malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma is exceptionally rare.
pitfalls: misdiagnosing the lesions as diffuse hepatic metastases and instituting unnecessary oncological treatment
failing to obtain MRCP, which best distinguishes them from communicating biliary disease
attributing abnormal liver tests to the hamartomas rather than seeking another cause
confusing them with microabscesses in a septic or immunocompromised patient
over-investigating an otherwise classic incidental finding
